briefing.question: What makes a result legitimate: strict adherence to the rules as written, or the widest possible participation? When may an authority bend a rule to save the purpose of the rule?

briefing.split: Aquinas, by proper authority; Rousseau, refusal is worse.

briefing.question: Can a protest movement become a government without losing what made it trustworthy? Is legitimacy earned by popular outrage, by institutions, or by competence?
briefing.agreed: A ballot win beats the street.
briefing.split: Machiavelli trusts the people; Plato, Burke wait to see them govern.

briefing.question: Does justice require order first, or is order without justice only a pause in conflict? Is disorder a cause or a symptom?
briefing.agreed: Violence must stop; order needs justice.
briefing.split: Hobbes, security first; King, grievances; Locke, rulers too.

briefing.question: Can a shared public space stay neutral on a moral question that one side experiences as a debate and the other as an attack on its dignity?
briefing.split: Mill, one rule for all; Popper, limit only force; Aristotle, civility.

briefing.question: Can education about contested questions ever be neutral, and who decides where informing ends and persuading begins?
briefing.split: Aristotle, public formation; Mill, both sides; Socrates, who judges?

briefing.question: Where does the right to offend end and incitement begin, and how can a plural society tolerate those it believes corrode its pluralism?
briefing.split: Mill, imminent danger; Ashoka, restraint; Locke, the peace.

briefing.question: Who owns a culture, and when does inspiration become taking? Is credit a matter of courtesy or of justice?
briefing.split: Jefferson, ideas unowned; Herder, Aquinas, credit as due.

briefing.question: Can the Church draw near to power without being used by it? Is the pastor's role to counsel the ruler in private or to testify against him in public?
briefing.agreed: A sacred act is no endorsement.
briefing.split: Ambrose, private counsel first; Calvin, correction as public as prayer.

briefing.question: When does a pastor's duty to speak about justice become telling people how to vote? Who may judge which political questions are moral absolutes and which are prudential?
briefing.split: Romero, name the danger; Leo XIII, Calvin, leave the vote to conscience.

briefing.question: How much diversity in worship can one communion bear before unity becomes uniformity, or diversity becomes division?
briefing.split: Vincent, what was always prayed; Gregory, gather good customs.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: who owns a culture, and when does inspiration become taking? Is credit a matter of courtesy or of justice? But truthfulness about origins is owed to those whose heritage is shown, because a false impression wrongs them.

Calvin wrote on the two governments, spiritual and political. Locke wrote on the separate spheres of church and commonwealth. opening.text: Tonight's subject: when does a pastor's duty to speak about justice become telling people how to vote, and who may judge which political questions are moral absolutes and which are prudential? The report notes that Gaudium et Spes allows the Church to pass moral judgment on politics when fundamental rights or salvation require it, while reminding lay people that pastors do not always hold concrete political solutions (Gaudium et Spes 76 and 43, paraphrased). The report gives one side, the signatories, as saying they cannot remain neutral, that silence before past totalitarian threats left a shameful legacy, and that the candidacy contradicts Catholic social teaching. The other side, critics including many of the 48 percent who voted for Bolsonaro, says tariffs, gun policy and foreign alliances are prudential questions on which faithful Catholics may differ, and that condemning one candidate without naming him is still taking a side. Leo XIII, you begin.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Vincent of Lérins wrote the rule the report names, what has been believed everywhere, always and by all, along with his allowance for real growth, so he speaks first. Ignatius of Antioch wrote, as the report names, that nothing in the Church be done without the bishop. Cyprian wrote On the Unity of the Church, also named. Gregory the Great wrote the letter, preserved by Bede, telling a missionary bishop to gather good customs from every church, the classic case for diversity under unity. Newman wrote on how a living tradition changes in order to remain the same. Pope Francis and Traditionis Custodes, named in the report, are in copyright and context only, as are the organizers and Vatican officials.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: how much diversity in worship can one communion bear before unity becomes uniformity, or diversity becomes division? The report gives one side, the organizers, as saying they are loyal to Peter, have a right to pray at his tomb with their ancestral liturgy, find the ban inexplicable, and note that other groups were allowed in. The other side, supporters of the restrictions following Traditionis Custodes, holds that the reformed liturgy is the one expression of the Roman Rite and that large public events can become demonstrations against it. The report found no public Vatican statement of its reasons, and we take no view on what they were. Vincent, you begin.

turn.text: The report names my rule, so let me give it in full. “in the Catholic Church itself, all possible care must be taken, that we hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all” (The Commonitory, ch. 2, §6) The organizers stand on it. Their liturgy, they say, is what the Church prayed for centuries, and what has been held so long and so widely cannot suddenly become suspect.

turn.text: But the report is right that I also allowed growth. I asked whether there is to be no progress in the Church, and answered that there should be much, “Yet on condition that it be real progress, not alteration of the faith.” (The Commonitory, ch. 23, §54) A child grows into a man and remains the same person. So my rule cuts two ways. It forbids treating the ancient rite as alien to the Church, and it forbids treating a reform as illegitimate merely because it is new, if it is true growth from the same root.

turn.text: But I also gave an image of unity that is not uniformity: “As there are many rays of the sun, but one light; and many branches of a tree, but one strength based in its tenacious root” (On the Unity of the Church, §5). The light is one; the rays are many. A Church can bear many rays, so long as none of them pretends to be a separate sun. The question both sides must ask is whether the traditional rite is a ray of the one light or is being made into a rival sun. If it is the first, it can be welcomed. If it is the second, it divides, whichever side makes it so.
